Catch My Drift
KACH my DRIFT
phrase (Boomer slang)
Drift in the sense of the general meaning or tendency of what someone says ("the drift of his argument") is old English, given by Webster in 1828. Catch my drift? / Get my drift? — "Do you understand what I’m getting at?" — is twentieth-century American colloquial, very common in the 1950s–70s, often with a wink that means the speaker is hinting rather than saying it outright.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Catch my drift? means "Do you understand what I’m getting at?" It is usually said after a hint rather than a plain statement, with a raised eyebrow. The Christian observation: the phrase is a small window into two biblical concerns — understanding and plain speech. On understanding: God wants His people to catch His drift. When Ezra read the law, the Levites "read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading" (Neh 8:8). Philip asked the Ethiopian, "Understandest thou what thou readest?" (Act 8:30). The Lord Jesus ended His parables with a summons to catch the drift: "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear" (Mat 13:9), and after the resurrection "opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures" (Luk 24:45). On plain speech: Paul insists that a speaker who is not understood is wasting breath: "except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air" (1Co 14:9). The wink in catch my drift sometimes hides a meaning the speaker would not want to say plainly — an innuendo, a threat, a hint of something improper. The Christian should prefer the open word. A father can use the phrase with a smile and still teach his children that God does not speak in winks; He has made His drift plain in His Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

Mid-20th-c. colloquial (on the 1828 drift, "meaning, tendency") for "Do you understand what I’m getting at?" — Scripture prizes understanding (Neh 8:8) and plain speech (1Co 14:9) over the wink.

expand to see more

CATCH MY DRIFT, phr. (American colloquial, 20th c.; common 1950s–70s) Do you understand what I mean? Often used after a hint or an indirect statement. Also get my drift.

Webster (1828) — DRIFT, noun 4. Course of any thing; tendency; aim; main force; as the drift of reasoning or argument; the drift of a discourse.

Decode for families: the Gen Z equivalent is "if you know, you know" — also a hint, also worth asking about.

Key Scripture

Neh 8:8 — "So they read in the book in the law of God distinctly, and gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading."

Act 8:30 — "And Philip ran thither to him, and heard him read the prophet Esaias, and said, Understandest thou what thou readest?"

Mat 13:9 — "Who hath ears to hear, let him hear."

Luk 24:45 — "Then opened he their understanding, that they might understand the scriptures,"

1Co 14:9 — "So likewise ye, except ye utter by the tongue words easy to be understood, how shall it be known what is spoken? for ye shall speak into the air."

Modern Corruption

A harmless colloquialism; its only shadow is the wink that hints at what one will not say plainly, and Scripture prefers words easy to be understood.

expand to see more

Most of the time catch my drift is simply friendly: "Are you following me?" But the phrase has a sly use too. A man hints at a bribe, an innuendo, or a threat and asks if you catch his drift, so that he can later deny having said anything. Scripture’s preference for plain speech (Mat 5:37; 1Co 14:9) cuts against that sly use. The godly man does not need a wink; he says what he means.

The phrase also reminds the Christian of his chief task as a hearer: to catch God’s drift. The Scriptures are not a code for insiders but a word given to be understood, and God gives teachers to explain it (Neh 8:8) and His Spirit to open the mind (Luk 24:45). A family that reads the Bible together and asks, "What is God getting at here?" is asking the right question.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English drifan (to drive) → drift (that which is driven; tendency, meaning; 1828) → 20th-c. colloquial catch / get my drift.

expand to see more

Old English drifan — to drive, to impel

Middle English drift — a driving; that which is driven, as snow

16th c.–: drift — the tendency or general meaning of speech (1828)

20th c.: catch my drift? / get my drift?

Greek syniēmi — to understand, to put together (Mat 13:15; Luk 24:45)

Usage

""Curfew is ten, and the car is mine, not yours. Catch my drift?" "Yes, sir.""

"They gave the sense, and caused them to understand the reading (Neh 8:8)."

"Who hath ears to hear, let him hear (Mat 13:9)."
